hints: Focus on what the two different tests are checking, solubility with strontium ions and reaction with an acid.
Remember that carbonate and hydrogencarbonate ions always fizz with dilute acids to give off colourless $\text{CO}_2$ gas.
Now compare chloride and sulfate with $\text{Sr}^{2+}$, only one forms an insoluble white strontium salt while the other stays in solution.
walkthrough:
**Start with the dilute acid test**

Think like a detective. Carbonates and hydrogencarbonates always react with $\text{H}^+$ to make $\text{CO}_2$ gas, which you would see as fizzing or effervescence.

$$\text{CO}_3^{2-} + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Rule out the fizzing ions**

R shows no visible reaction with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$. That means no gas is made, so R cannot contain $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ or $\text{HCO}_3^-$.

This leaves only $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ as possibilities.

**Use the strontium nitrate test**

Now look at solubility. All Group 2 chlorides are soluble, so $\text{SrCl}_2$ stays dissolved and gives no precipitate.

$$\text{Sr}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Cl}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{SrCl}_2(aq) \text{, no precipitate}$$

**Confirm the sulfate precipitate**

Strontium sulfate is insoluble in water and forms a white precipitate. This matches the observation perfectly.

$$\text{Sr}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{SrSO}_4(s) \text{, white precipitate}$$

**Conclude the anion**

Only sulfate gives a white precipitate with $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ and no reaction with dilute acid. So the anion in R must be sulfate.

options.A: Incorrect. Chloride would indeed show no reaction with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$, but $\text{SrCl}_2$ is soluble so no white precipitate would form with $\text{Sr(NO}_3)_2$. Students who forget Group 2 chloride solubility often pick this.
options.B: Correct. $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ forms insoluble white $\text{SrSO}_4$ with $\text{Sr}^{2+}$, and sulfate does not react with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ to give a gas or precipitate, matching both observations.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{HCO}_3^-$ would react with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ to give visible effervescence of $\text{CO}_2$, and strontium hydrogencarbonate is soluble so no precipitate is expected. This contradicts both observations.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ would give a white precipitate of $\text{SrCO}_3$ with $\text{Sr}^{2+}$, but it would also fizz vigorously with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ to give $\text{CO}_2$. The second observation rules it out.
